spoken_math: In Indian English mathematics classrooms, instruction is delivered in English using characteristic classroom phrasing. Transcript prose names mathematical, scientific, and technical vocabulary in the book language matching the printed textbook, while the explanation variety carries ordinary teaching language. Tutors never translate a book term instead, keeping all technical terms in English as printed in the textbook. Because the explanation variety is Indian English and the book language is English, both the explanatory prose and the spoken readings are carried in English using Indian English classroom conventions. The standard teaching register is informal classroom speech. A formal register, specifically formal textbook English, is allowed only when reading aloud printed textbook definitions, official theorem statements, or formal examination question prompts verbatim; tutors switch register only on those specific occasions, choosing formal phrasing instead of everyday operational words. Number words for numerals are spoken as: 0 is "zero", 1 is "one", 2 is "two", 3 is "three", 4 is "four", 5 is "five", 6 is "six", 7 is "seven", 8 is "eight", 9 is "nine", 10 is "ten", 11 is "eleven", 12 is "twelve", 13 is "thirteen", 14 is "fourteen", 15 is "fifteen", 16 is "sixteen", 17 is "seventeen", 18 is "eighteen", 19 is "nineteen", 20 is "twenty", 30 is "thirty", 40 is "forty", 50 is "fifty", 60 is "sixty", 70 is "seventy", 80 is "eighty", 90 is "ninety", 100 is "one hundred", 1000 is "one thousand", 100000 is "one lakh", and 10000000 is "one crore". The decimal point is spoken as "point", and negative values are prefixed with "minus". For multiplication, tutors use distinct expressions: "into" is the primary operational word used during step-by-step arithmetic and algebraic derivation; "multiplied by" is reserved for the formal register when reading definitions or question text; "cross" is used strictly for vector cross products; "dot" is used strictly for vector dot products; and "times" is used when scaling parenthetical expressions. For division and fractions, "upon" is the standard classroom term for algebraic fractions and ratios; "by" is used for simple numerical fractions and calculus differentials; "whole upon" is used when a compound numerator with multiple terms is divided by a denominator; "whole by" is used as an alternate phrasing for expressions with compound numerators; and "divided by" is reserved for formal enunciation. For powers, "square" and "cube" are used for exponents two and three on single terms; "whole square" and "whole cube" are used when a multi-term grouped expression is raised to the second or third power; "raised to" is used for higher or variable exponents; "raise to" is used during rapid spoken derivation; and "to the power" is used in formal reading. For roots, tutors say "root" during active problem solving, "under root" when emphasizing terms situated beneath the radical bar, "square root of" in the formal register, "cube root of" for third roots, and "nth root of" for general radical indices. For equality and relational operators, tutors say "is equal to" in formal statements, "equals to" in colloquial chalkboard explanation, "equals" during rapid algebraic transitions, "not equal to" for inequality, "less than" for strict lower bound, "greater than" for strict upper bound, "less than or equal to" for non-strict lower bound, "greater than or equal to" for non-strict upper bound, "approximately equal to" for approximations, and "plus or minus" for dual signs. Logical connectives and symbols are read as "implies" for logical deduction, "which gives" when showing sequential algebraic results, "therefore" for concluding deductions, "since" for stating premises, "belongs to" for set membership, "does not belong to" for non-membership, "infinity" for unbounded limits, and "percent" for percentages. Grouping delimiters are spoken as "bracket open" and "bracket close" for parentheses, "square bracket open" and "square bracket close" for square brackets, "curly bracket open" and "curly bracket close" for braces, and "mod" for absolute value bars. In calculus, tutors pronounce the derivative as "dy by dx" during working steps and "derivative of y with respect to x" when reciting the formal definition, while limits use "limit" and "tends to". Variables are pronounced using English alphabet names, with the letter z consistently pronounced "zed", the letter h pronounced "aitch" or "haitch", and uppercase variables distinguished by the prefix "capital". Standard Greek letters are pronounced by academic names: "alpha", "beta", "gamma", "theta", "lambda", "mu", "pi", "sigma", "phi", and "omega". Regarding words from another language, tutors occasionally employ informal conversational markers such as "na" or "theek hai" during casual classroom exchanges, but all mathematical operations and technical vocabulary strictly use English words. Here are representative classroom examples: To solve the quadratic equation, we apply the quadratic formula: <math spoken="x equals minus b plus or minus root b square minus four a c whole upon two a">x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}</math>. Substituting the coefficients gives <math spoken="x equals minus five plus or minus root twenty-five minus twenty-four whole upon two">x = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{25 - 24}}{2}</math>, which simplifies to <math spoken="x equals minus five plus or minus one whole upon two">x = \frac{-5 \pm 1}{2}</math>. Therefore, we obtain two values: <math spoken="x equals minus two">x = -2</math> and <math spoken="x equals minus three">x = -3</math>. In calculus, we differentiate the product: <math spoken="y equals bracket open x plus two bracket close whole square into bracket open three x minus one bracket close">y = (x + 2)^2 (3x - 1)</math>. Taking the derivative with respect to x gives <math spoken="dy by dx equals two into bracket open x plus two bracket close into bracket open three x minus one bracket close plus three into bracket open x plus two bracket close whole square">\frac{dy}{dx} = 2(x + 2)(3x - 1) + 3(x + 2)^2</math>. Finally, for limits we write: <math spoken="limit x tends to zero sine of five x whole upon x equals five">\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(5x)}{x} = 5</math>.
spoken_chemistry: In Indian English chemistry classrooms, chemical formulas, equations, and reactions are spoken using English letter names, standard number words, and established classroom conventions. Transcript prose names mathematical, scientific, and technical vocabulary in the book language matching the printed textbook, while the explanation variety carries ordinary teaching language. Tutors never translate a book term instead, keeping all chemical nomenclature, element names, and reaction terminology in English as printed in the textbook. Because chemistry shares the same spoken variety and number words as mathematics, leading coefficients use the identical number words, and the connective plus between chemical reactants or products is spoken as "plus". Chemical symbols are read letter by letter by their English names. Numerical subscripts attached directly to individual elements are spoken as cardinal numbers immediately following the element letter name without inserting the word subscript. When a polyatomic group enclosed in parentheses carries a subscript of two, tutors read the bracketed group followed by "twice"; when it carries a subscript of three, tutors read the bracketed group followed by "thrice" or "taken thrice". Leading coefficients are read directly as cardinal numbers preceding the substance, and tutors occasionally insert "moles of" during stoichiometric analysis. Physical states of matter written in parentheses after a formula are read as full words: s is "solid", l is "liquid", g is "gas", and aq is "aqueous". Reaction arrows are read with distinct words depending on classroom focus: "gives" is used during step-by-step equation balancing and board work; "forms" is used when highlighting product synthesis; and "yields" is used in formal reading of textbook problem statements. Equilibrium arrows are read as "in equilibrium with" or "reversible reaction with". An upward arrow indicating gas evolution is spoken as "gas evolved" or "gas liberated", while a downward arrow indicating precipitation is spoken as "precipitate formed" or "ppt formed". Reaction conditions written above the arrow are read explicitly: the symbol delta is spoken as "on heating", and a specified catalyst is read as "in the presence of". Ionic charges and oxidation states are read with the magnitude followed by the sign, such as "positive" or "negative" for single charges, and "two plus" or "two minus" for divalent ions. Here are representative classroom examples: When calcium hydroxide reacts with hydrochloric acid in aqueous solution, neutralization proceeds as follows: <math spoken="C a O H twice aqueous plus two H C l aqueous gives C a C l two aqueous plus two H two O liquid">\text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)</math>. Solid calcium carbonate undergoes thermal decomposition: <math spoken="C a C O three solid on heating gives C a O solid plus C O two gas">\text{CaCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\uparrow</math>. In single displacement, iron reacts with copper sulfate solution: <math spoken="F e solid plus C u S O four aqueous gives F e S O four aqueous plus C u solid">\text{Fe}(s) + \text{CuSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)</math>, which gives the net ionic form <math spoken="F e solid plus C u two plus aqueous gives F e two plus aqueous plus C u solid">\text{Fe}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)</math>. For the industrial synthesis of ammonia, the reversible reaction is written as: <math spoken="N two gas plus three H two gas in equilibrium with two N H three gas">\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)</math>.
